utterances.text: Was it immediately after she was identified as an SDA woman that you say that she was grabbed and killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: When he said what he had to say, I mean the one with the ponytail, the one with the long hair, when he told -- that is, Adolf said, "We've got a woman, a balija woman, a member of the SDA." Then he started for her, got her by the scruff of her neck, pulled her down at the edge. He made her go down on her knees, and fired a bullet into the back of her head. Then that one with long hair told us, "Get into the warehouse," and we entered the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went inside the warehouse, were there other people inside the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon entering the warehouse, how many people were inside it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, out there, in the corner, there were people -- well, there could have been some 20 or so in the corner down there. I didn't go to count them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by reference to, as it were, going inside the door, where inside the hangar were the people placed? Were they placed on the left-hand side, the right-hand side? Where, exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right-hand side. There were people -- as I am sitting, as I go into the warehouse, they were on the right-hand side. In a corner up there, there were some socks, there were socks and white things, I mean shirts and T-shirts, and that is where those people were sitting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right, Mr. E, that when you went inside the hangar, apart from persons being detained there, there was at least one, if not more, police officers inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: A policeman in a short-sleeved shirt, he was standing at the warehouse as I went in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second person that you saw being assaulted, the allegation against him was that he was a Croat who was also a rapist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's why he was singled out for being kicked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was separated out down to a corner at the bottom of the warehouse. That's where he was sitting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people in the hangar at this time, were they exclusively men, or men and women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were only men in the hangar where I was, in this storage room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person who was kicked, was he in fact a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: The one who was down in the corner?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the one who was accused of being a rapist.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He was down there in the corner, and when they set me down in the chair, this policeman said he raped a nine-year old girl who was Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to another particular individual. You recognised someone, amongst the people, who was already detained there, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: I only knew one person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the person who'd worked as a nurse at a medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that was my neighbour. But this young man was -- he was one of the two who were giving us food, and this neighbour of mine was distributing the bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a neighbour of yours who was acting as a, as it were, like a cook, or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. He wasn't a cook. No, he was just distributing food to the detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to be absolutely clear as to who we're talking about. You were asked this yesterday by my learned friend from the Prosecution: "Was there a man present who had been a male nurse at the hospital?" And you said, "He was the one distributing food." Is that correct or incorrect, that information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: The male nurse did distribute food, and I reconfirmed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he the nurse who had worked at the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the person who had been the nurse at the medical centre? Just tell us that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: This policeman came and called him out and started beating him up to the door. And at the door, as this door was opened, there were two men there. As he reached the door, he was hit in the chest. He fell, and then there was -- you could just hear his moans, and you could hear this "duuu" [phoen] sound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see what happened; you could only hear those things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: I just heard; didn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you cannot say in fact if that person was killed or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't see him being killed. I just heard the shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is this: In your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you then describe a second victim, who you describe as the person who was there as a cook and who had been giving out food, giving out bread for you to eat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to suggest to you is that your recollection is very confused about these incidents, Mr. E.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: What kind of confusion?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, again, in evidence yesterday before the Tribunal -- I'm sorry. Forgive me. You describe the second person also as a male nurse.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were both male nurses. There were two male nurses, and this is what I repeat now. There were two male nurses, and they were both taken out, and both of them were shot, the same way; first beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, in relation to the second person, does it come to this: Having been beaten, the person was taken out, and you did not see them again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, the person did not come back, and you never saw them again. They never came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you heard a shot, you don't know precisely what happened to the person who was taken out, because you were not present?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've already asked that question, Mr. Greaves. I believe that the witness has answered you. The witness said that he did not see the scene exactly; he said that he heard cries and he heard gunfire. He can't say anything more than that. Let's try to move forward, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the case, that in relation to that man, he was selected by somebody called "Sok"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sok? No. Sok was doing this thing to the Croatian person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to put to you is that, in fact, what you told the Office of the Prosecutor was this: He was pointed out by Sok, beaten with a stick by a young police officer, and then taken outside the hangar. But you now say that that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: The policeman with a short-sleeved blue uniform was -- it was a blue uniform. I will repeat it 100 times. This is the man who was bringing men out. Sok stood at the door. That was the one with the long hair. And I can repeat it 100 times, and I will continue to repeat it. Please do not go on like that, because I will always repeat it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this right, that one of the people who was taken out during the course of that evening was accused of being a sniper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. His name was Braco. He was from Grcica. He had been accused of being a sniper, and he was taken out and killed in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, did you see him being killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I just heard. I just told you, it was the same way in which these two food persons were. He never came back into the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you subsequently -- I'm sorry. Were you subsequently interrogated, yourself, Mr. E?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: This policeman came to me and told me, "You, yellow, come on," because I had this colour shirt on me. And when I got going, he started beating me with his baton and said, "Run," and I kept running. And as I reached the door, I could only hear -- I could only feel two feet kicking me. And then I just fell, and then they were just kicking me. And the one with the ponytail told me to get up. I got up. I thought that I was going to the office where I had turned in my documents. And then he hit me, and he said, "Not there; over here." And then I saw that people were going into the toilet, and I thought, "Well, most probably they will kill me here in this toilet." And I walked in, and there was a door straight down. He walked me in there, and then men were sitting around the table. They were in military uniform, some in SMB-type uniform and the others camouflage-type uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. E, you were issued with the pass in due course, but before then, had there been some form of questioning of you or discussion about you that took place in your presence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were hitting me, and this man walked me into this room, this office, and I saw there were nine of them, and the tenth man was Adolf. One was sitting in an armchair, one was sitting on a table. Black T-shirts and black jeans. He did not ask me, he just pushed me against the wardrobe, and he asked Adolf, "Is he going to work with me or is he going to work with the other men?" And then Adolf told him, "Go on, Sasa."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was somebody in the room whom you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Adolf was sitting in a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but apart from him, there was somebody that you knew in that room, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, but I just want to explore a little the conversation that took place. He recognised you and told those other people in the room about you; is that what it comes to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, when I was being beaten. He said to this Adolf, "Adolf, don't beat him. He is a poor man." And Adolf said, "How do you mean, a poor man?" And he said, "Well, he is just a poor man who is trying to make ends meet. (redacted) (redacted). He is just trying to survive and feed his family." And this is when Adolf gave me a pass so I can get out of the camp and I could take care of my wife and child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it also the case that part of the discussion and the reason why you were released was because you were identified as having nothing to do with the Muslim political parties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know, but he just said that I had been 100 per cent investigated, and then he released me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason I asked you that last question, Mr. E, and so that you may deal with it, is what you told the Office of the Prosecutor and put into your statement was this: "(redacted) 15 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)." So it's right, isn't it --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the reason why you were released --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- is because you were not associated with politics in any way? And that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point, the beating stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me point out to you, Mr. Greaves -- this is in paragraph 16 of the Prosecutor's report -- we don't have to repeat what is clear. Goran said that the witness was just a poor man who had nothing to do with politics. That's in the report. Spare the witness a bit, please. When something was said, it was said, and it seems to me that that's in this summary that I've got right in front of me, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The pass that was issued to you, signed with this name, "Adolf," at any time during your detention in Luka on that day had you learnt the name "Adolf" from him, apart from seeing it on the pass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because Sok addressed him as "Adolf."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't learn his real name that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much later did you associate the name "Goran Jelisic" with the name "Adolf"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: When people came from the camp and they talked about him, they said that his name was Goran Jelisic and that his nickname was Adolf. This is when I learned his real name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were relying on what other people told you. You don't -- you, yourself, do not know how they came to be in possession of the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, those who were in the camp, I don't know. I know that Adolf -- that Adolf, even today, or when we reached free territory, when those who were released came to the free territory, they were talking about Adolf from the camp being Goran Jelisic, so this is what I can reconfirm about Adolf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put the question to you in another way. You cannot say the circumstances in which they, your informants, learnt this name and whether the information they were given was accurate, can you? Because you weren't present when that happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know his real a name. I did not know his real name, and I cannot say what I did not know, so I'm only saying about what I did know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to suggest to you is that whoever it was who signed that, and was described as Adolf, was not Goran Jelisic, and the description which you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, I suggest, indicates that you've got the wrong person, because you described someone who is far taller than he is. So you're mistaken as to his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, I've noted on several occasions that you proceed with affirmations. I ask you to ask your question and to keep your opinions for your final conclusions. You cannot intimidate the witness by saying, "I assert this. I assert that." No, you've got to be more nuanced. You have the right to your opinions, but you can express them in your final pleadings or, when you do so, do it with a degree of nuance, showing the witness that there may be contradictions of what he is saying. But you cannot begin by saying, "I assert this" or "I assert that." I ask you to be careful, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I suspect, Your Honour, that it's one of these things that come from a matter of the different styles that exist in different systems. And just as I have to be tolerant of the civil-law system and their practice, of course, it would be helpful if a similar tolerance was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not applying civil or Roman law. I'm sorry, Mr. Greaves, we're not going to go back to that discussion. In this Court, we don't have Anglo-Saxon or civil law. You seem to say that we're only using civil law. We have one law, and it's in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and you will note that each time I make a comment, I rely on the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I am not contesting at all your right to conduct your cross-examination as you like; I'm simply asking that when you proceed with assertions, to do it with nuance and to show each time why you are doing it. That is your right. As regards the rest, your opinions, you will have ample time to express them at the time of the final pleadings. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put the question in another way, then, to you, Mr. E. The person you have described as being one metre 90 tall and identified as Adolf, identifying him as Goran Jelisic, you have made a mistake. Do you accept that or not, Mr. E?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you understand the question that was asked -- properly, and I thank Mr. Greaves for that -- did you understand the sense of the question that was asked? Mr. Greaves is asking whether you consider that you made a mistake when you associated the first name "Adolf" with the man that you alluded to specifically. Did you understand the question? Try to concentrate, and then please answer. You must answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: I say that he is tall, that his height was between 180 and 190 centimetres. He was thin, skinny; that is how he looked then. I was very afraid, so I didn't approach him to try to take his measurements. Had I been able to take his measurements, I could have been able to tell you exactly, but if you came close enough, you could tell what was lying in wait for you; you would get a bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want just to clarify something about this pass that you were issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You left the Luka detention facility and went where, exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Exactly where I went? This Goran from Grcica put me in a car and drove me home. To give it exact information, Goran put me in a car and drove me home to Grcica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had your family gone already or were they still there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, sir, they had not left. They were there. When my wife kept -- gave me -- dressed my eyes throughout the night so that I could see again, and then in the morning, I took my child by the hand and crossed the lines. It is better to try to escape than to wait for a bullet. Let's try to finish this off, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you used that pass in order to make your way through the lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let's get this straight, sir. There were two lines. There were Serbian lines and the Muslim lines. I took a risk. It was either to be killed or to cross over with my wife. I crossed over, and I arrived in the free territory, and this is where I was found by our men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. E, you've just asked us to get a move on, and now you're not answering the question. Did you or did you not use that pass that you had been given, to show it to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, I never used it anywhere. I did not use the pass anywhere, because I had no opportunity to use it. To whom should I produce it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But eventually the pass was handed over to somebody, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I turned it in when I arrived in the free territory. I turned it over to a man -- I did not have any other documents. I had that document. Had I known about this, I would have eaten the document. I wouldn't have shown it to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next time that you saw that pass was when it was shown to you by somebody from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: The next time, after the pass was taken away from me in the free territory, it was shown to me here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person to whom -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleagues and I are going to order a break now for two reasons. I would like that the parties in this courtroom focus -- well, I'm turning to you, Witness E. All of this is extremely painful, and I want you to understand that the Judges are listening to you with a great deal of attention and have a great deal of sympathy for what happened to you. At the same time, we must do our work as Judges, that is, to be sure that the accused, who is here, be properly defended under conditions that, in civilised countries, are called an equitable and fair trial, even if you experienced dreadful and tragic experiences and the fact that people who were murdered next to you did not have the right to a fair trial. Nonetheless, I'm going to ask you to rest for 15 minutes. Mr. Greaves, I would like to say to you, in agreement with my colleagues, and remind you of what you already know, that at the basis of this trial, there has been a plea of guilt asserted very clearly by the accused, who is present here, and I return you to the indictment. We are only discussing count 1, which is genocide. Through questions that are asked, I would not like us to go back, in summary, to the presence of Jelisic in the hangar or the confusion between him and other people. With all the care required and with all your great skill, I would like to refer you to the need to observe the fact that there was a plea of guilt, and I have it in front of me. We can look at counts 2 and 3, the killings of -- I won't say their names. Perhaps they were a protected witness, four other men. Counts 4 and 5, the killing of an unknown male; counts 6 and 7, the killing of HJ. I won't say. Counts 8 and 9, the killing of a man from Sinteraj; 10 and 11, the killing of AH or H; 12 and 13, the killing of S; 14 and 15, the killing of SC and JC; 16 and 17, the killing of H and SZ; 18 and 19, the killing of MB; counts 20 and 21, the killing of MA; 22 and 23, the killing of SG; 24 and 25, the killing of S; counts 26 and 27, the killing of MG; counts 28 and 29, sexual assault. No, those are not ascribed. No, they relate to the co-accused. 30 and 31, and I could even add 32 and 33, not 34 and 35, but 36 and 37, 38, 39, 40 and 41, and that's it, and 44. I do understand that in order to demonstrate your client's innocence in respect of genocide, that you are using all types of details as regards the counts of genocide, but I would like -- we are going to take our 15-minute break, but I would like you to consider the fact that there are certain things that have been acknowledged, that is, all these murders that your client has acknowledged, if you agree. And I'm going to ask the Victims and Witnesses Section take particular care of Witness E. I'm going to give you 15 minutes, and if we have to take 20 minutes, then we'll take 20 minutes. We're going to take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness E, how do you feel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you properly taken care of during the break?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was somebody. There was somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you continue? We're going to try to finish this as quickly as we can. Will you be all right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Greaves, do you have much longer to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really would like you to try to go as quickly as you can, given the condition of the witness. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I say, of course, if you can. I'm not saying you must, but given the psychological and physical condition of the witness, I'm simply asking, if you can, to go as quickly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think one more question about the pass, and then I think we shall be on to the question of the list of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I mean it's a fair estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. E, I would like you just to look briefly at the exhibit that was shown to you this morning, which is the pass which bears your name. 24, please. Thank you. If I could just have a look at it as it goes past. Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only put the copy without the name -- only put the copy of it without the name on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Has that got his name on it? If so, please don't put it on the ELMO. All I want you to do is show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave him the document which has the name of the individual redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Take it off the ELMO, please, and just show it to the witness. All I want to do is show it to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. E, is that what was shown to you in April 1998 by Mr. Bernard O'Donnell, the investigator, effectively a copy of an original?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: A copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your own knowledge, you cannot say what has happened to the original or where the original is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm finished with the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. E, we're going to conclude, and as I've indicated to Their Honours in about 15 or 20 minutes, by asking you some questions about the people on the list you were asked about yesterday. Do you remember going through that list with the Prosecutor and being asked questions about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew of Stipo Glavocevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did you hear about what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: From people who were exchanged. It is from them that I heard it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as Suad Hodzic is concerned, you knew him before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He lived in Klanac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your information that was given to you was that he had been killed at the health centre. Can you remember who it was who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: People talk, but that is not the one that you mentioned. It is another Hodzic. But Papa, the one -- where it says "Papa", he is Hodzic too, and about him is that I heard he was killed in the health centre, whatever it was. It was about Papa that I heard that, because everybody says how he was tortured and tortured and tortured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did also know Suad Hodzic? I'm looking at your evidence --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. That is the guy from Klanac, and Papa is from Kolobara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we may clarify it, what did you hear about Suad Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: That he was killed at Luka, Suad. And Papa, Papa Hodzic, that he was killed at the health centre. But I don't know that because it is all hearsay, and I asked not to have to talk about that because I did not see it personally and I had nothing to do with it. What I saw, I will repeat it, and I'm positive about it 100 per cent. But what I didn't see, I mean I can't do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. We understand entirely, Mr. E, that what you are doing is reporting things which were told to you. We're just having a look at --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the reliability and accuracy of your information, because it may be important. All right? So please bear with me. I just need your help just to tell us how you've come by the information. Suljo Pezerovic --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Suljo Pezerovic is from Rijeka. He is a man from Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, your information was that he had been killed at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But again you knew nothing of that personally; you're relying on other people's information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of those three people we've now discussed, did you know anything of their political affiliations before the war? Were they involved in politics, members of political parties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know only about Papa, that he was a member of the SDA, Papa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Rahim Redenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Simply that he was killed, and I'm afraid the transcript from which I've been working, it isn't quite clear where he was killed because there was one of the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard that he was killed at Es.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts is that? I'm sorry, I don't know the geography well enough, so please help us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Where is that? Well, as you go from the centre of the town and head for Bijeljina, and then there comes the school, and then the forest management, and you turn right, and it is those new buildings in Brcko which were built and called Es.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's effectively a small suburb of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's not a suburb, it's still the centre of Brcko, except that these are new buildings and they called it Es, E-S. You can enter from Bijeljina, but then you come from Tuzla, then via Majevica and that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he had been involved in politics in any way before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, and we're drawing towards the end, Mr. E, so that you know, Kibe Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Kibe, Kibe. He was a butcher in Brcko. (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he involved in politics at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again you were told that he had been killed, and you described it as in some bowling lanes is what I've got in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the collection centre where people go bowling. That's what I heard, that it was there. But that man was never actively involved in politics. He was actively involved in bottles. He liked to drink, that Kibe, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally Osman Vatic --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Osman Vatic is a lawyer, famous Brcko lawyer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear about him, and when did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: After people were exchanged, after they arrived from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I appreciate that, Mr. Greaves. I appreciate your having tried to go as quickly as you could for the cross-examination. Mr. Nice, do you have some additional questions to ask or no further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've got no further questions to ask. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me turn to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Witness E, good morning. I can't call you by your name, so allow me to say just "E". I'm rather confused by the pass you gave us, which indicates that you were 100 per cent clean, and I suppose the word "clean" in English is not the same thing in French. I suppose it is the right translation of the Serbo-Croat, which is "Cist", is it? How do you say it in Serbo Croat? Is the word "clean" right here? I assume it is right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What is the significance of being clean? What makes a person clean, to have such a pass? That's my first question. I tried to find out for myself, from your answers, and you mentioned in passing, very modestly, that you were just a miserable wretch, very modestly, of course, which you are not, but does that mean that others were unimportant, because that means unimportant, unimportant in the Muslim community, were considered clean because they are miserable wretches, as you said? What makes some clean and others not clean? That's the question, if you can answer it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think -- well, he wrote that he had checked me. When this little Goran from Grcica told him, "Don't, Adolf, he is a poor man. (redacted) (redacted)" and he wrote on the pass that he had checked me 100 per cent, that nobody should let his finger on me, that I could move freely around the town, and that is what he wrote. He told me, "Here is this pass for you. Whoever you show this pass to, he won't harm you in any way." That is the only answer I know how to give you. I don't know other things. I have no education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You have done all right. So, the fact that you were spared because you were a poor man, which means that poor people were spared? Is that the only thing in your mind, that because you were poor, you were spared out of charity, and those who were not poor were not spared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here, that young one, that Goran, he saved me, and I can never thank him enough. But I believe that he did not know who was rich and who was poor. He did not know that. People were simply killed, and it was Adolf himself who told me before that, "You're going home. Nobody left this place alive, but you are going home to provide for your wife and child." That is what Adolf told me. I have nothing else to say. And he wrote that for me and gave me this pass, and I never even looked at it. I put it in my pocket. My wife took it and put it in her purse, and we crossed the lines, we escaped across the lines, reached the free territory. They asked for my identity card. I didn't have the identity card, and my wife said, "He doesn't have the identity card because he was in the camp in Luka, but he does have this pass." It is with this pass that I reached the free territory, and I know nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just to sum up, he told you, "You, alone, are going to be spared"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was completely an individual act. Thank you very much. That's all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness E. We are really finished now. I know that you're very tired. Before you leave, the Witness and Victims Unit will take care of you. You're not just going to go that way?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you taking the plane back home tonight? Is it tonight? Is your departure scheduled for tonight? Don't give me any specifics, but is it scheduled for tonight? Can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know when I'm leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, we're going to be sure that your departure takes place as best it can. We would like to express all our gratitude to you for having come here two times, and for having to recount all of these dreadful experiences, and to be confronted with the looks in this Tribunal of different people. Try to find peace again. You're going to leave this courtroom. We're going to draw the blinds so you're not recognised, and we hope that the remainder of your life is serene and good. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher not to bring the next witness in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher not to bring the next witness in until I've dealt with an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While we wait for the usher, may I cross the floor and hand a document to Mr. Greaves. Your Honour, what I have and what I've shown to Mr. Greaves is the documentation that explains our possession of the pass. I notice that there was a question asked that, of course, the witness couldn't answer about what happened to the pass or how it came into the possession of the OTP, and I would ask Your Honour to have a look at this document, which is an original with English and French translation. The original of this document will be somewhere here in the vaults and can be produced, if necessary, but it came associated with the pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We're going to keep this exhibit confidential. Can you bring in the next witness, please, Mr. Prosecutor, unless Mr. Greaves has any comments to make. I don't want this pass to spoil our whole day. It was the subject of many, many questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm still concerned about the accurate translation of the word which has been subject of discussion. Although we may have had a literal translation of it, there is some dispute as to what the idiomatic use of that phrase actually means, and I would invite the Tribunal to take some steps to have further investigation of the idiomatic use of this phrase, because my interpreter, and I'm not going to give evidence, but my interpreter has a suggestion, which what I'm going to suggest is that my interpreter and the head of the interpretation section of the Tribunal should meet and discuss what a definitive meaning of the word is in its idiomatic sense so that it may properly be dealt with. Your Honours have been exercised about it, and the word is important, and Your Honour Judge Riad has plainly picked it up and wants it clarified. I would invite its proper clarification, rather than just simply a literal translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Tribunal considers that it has received enough information about this. Mr. Prosecutor, would you bring in the next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tochilovsky will be calling the next witness, who seeks no protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Tochilovsky. All right. You're going to have the next witness brought in. It is now a quarter to 1:00, and we're going to have the next witness brought into the courtroom so that we can at least begin, and then continue on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to give us your family name, your first name, your place and date of birth, your current residence, and then you're going to take an oath according to a statement that is going to be given to you by the usher. First please give us your family name, your first name, your date of birth, place of birth, residence, and current occupation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm Amir Didic. I was born on the 1st of May, 1967, in Palanka, and I still live there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't get the interpretation -- yes, very well. Thank you. Please read the solemn declaration that is being given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may now be seated. Thank you for having come. You are a witness called by the Office of the Prosecutor in a trial which the Prosecutor has initiated against Goran Jelisic, who is in this courtroom. First you're going to answer the Prosecutor's questions, then the Defence will ask you some questions in what we call the cross-examination, and the Judges may also have some questions, if they so desire. Mr. Tochilovsky, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the witness may have a summary of his statements placed before him, if the usher would help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Tochilovsky:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Didic is this document before you the document that was shown to you recently and that you were able to read?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this the document you recognised as a correct summary of your statements?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, were you arrested by Serb soldiers at a road checkpoint and taken to the SUP in Brcko on May 19, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you detained in room 13 in Brcko police station?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other Muslim detainees in room 13 with you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were about four or five people there when I came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all of you then taken to the Luka detention camp and placed in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity were those people who were taken with you to Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, were you interrogated in Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court of the interrogation which took place on May 20, the next day you arrived at Luka, to Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I was brought there on the 19th of May, that is, to Luka. On the 20th of May, they began to interrogate me. I was first interrogated by two inspectors wearing multi-coloured uniforms, in one of the offices across the hangar, and then I was taken back to the hangar and then transferred to the other part of the hangar. There were doors between parts of the hangar. In the evening, Kole began to interrogate me, and there was also Dragan, a policeman -- I mean, he was an active-duty policeman before the war -- and there were a couple of people more whom I did not know, I mean, whom I had never seen before. The only one I knew was that policeman, Dragan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Goran Jelisic participate in the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any female among the interrogators?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a girl called Monika.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Monika before the war?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I used to see her. I did not really know her, but I used to see her. She worked for a coffee shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about her relationship with Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I knew nothing before that, but during my detention, I heard that they were living together and that they were friends -- or rather that they dated together. They were together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you treated during that interrogation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Very bad. Very badly. They beat me. They beat me with the baton, they kicked me, and they were wearing soldiers' boots, and things of that sort. All sorts of things: hands, fists. They forced me to make the sign of the cross and to change my name from Amir into Alexander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they made you make a cross, just with regard to that, you are a Muslim by ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Jelisic and other interrogators use any objects to beat you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Goran used it most. He used the baton. He used a piece of cable a couple of times. He broke Coca-Cola bottles against my head. Once he hit me with the fire hose. He hit me on the head so that I fainted. He was the one who beat me most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who? Can you give the name of the person you just mentioned? Who beat you the most?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic beat me the most, at least, that is how they addressed him. That is what they called him, Goran Jelisic or Adolf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Monika say anything to you when she participated in the beating?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, they cursed balijas' mothers, saying they should kill us all. She kept saying, "Why don't you kill him? Why are you discussing with him?" That was what Monika was saying to Goran.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, were other detainees beaten that evening, May 20, in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Andrija Tujekcic was taken there with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten again later the same evening?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who participated in that beating?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D, were you beaten the next day, 21st May?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Goran Jelisic and Monika participate in that beating?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How severe was that beating? Did you bleed? Did you have any injuries?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was bleeding. My lips had burst, and I had a bleeding nose, and my eyes, also, my eyes were all inflamed because of the blows by the fists and boots and everything, so my head was swollen, my ears were swollen. My head was impossible, really, and I was bleeding through the nose and through the mouth and teeth and all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Monika mistreat you inside the hangar, while you were lying in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion, I was lying down there after Goran had beat me with those pieces of the fire hose, when I fainted in the office. And I don't know what happened after that, whether somebody carried me to the hangar or what happened; I don't remember that. And then they covered me with something, with a cover. It was very hot, and of course there were flies all around. And at some point Monika entered to see if I was still alive, and poured some liquid over me, but my eyes were already closed because of the beating, so I couldn't see what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, for how many days did those interrogations and beatings last?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: It went on from between the 20th and 28th or 29th May, until the shift was changed, when Goran and the rest of them who were there left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many times a day were you taken out and beaten during this period?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Three times a day. That was the number of times that Goran and the others took me out and beat me. But Goran did that the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how many times you were beaten by Jelisic in camp, among other beatings during this period of time, how many times Goran participated in these beatings?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Ten to fifteen times, approximately. I cannot tell you the exact number of times, but about that number of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, was there a man named Ohro in Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he beat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether he was given any authority to beat prisoners by anyone?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, Goran Jelisic authorised him to do so, as did Monika. They sort of gave him a title of inspector. They sort of took pleasure in looking on as he was beating people like Tufekcic and me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, did you hear Jelisic saying why he had come to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, it was night time, he came in. He was cursing the Muslim mothers, and he was just verbally abusing everybody. And he said that "I came to Brcko with the intention of killing as many Muslims as possible." But, he said, "I just came from the Sava bridge; I just saved a Muslim. I am humane. I saved a Muslim; he had a wife and two children. I also am saving people, but I came here to kill as many Muslims as possible in Brcko."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to that Sava River bridge, when he said that he had saved a Bosnian or a Muslim, did he mention what happened to others on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, he said that he had killed them all, but that one man was crying and telling him how he had a wife and two children, and he saved him, but all the others were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, can you tell the Court who was a formal commander in the camp after May 19 when you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Kole, as warden of Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Goran Jelisic's role in camp at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Kole was some kind of a warden, but Goran Jelisic was authorised to do whatever he wanted to, as well as Monika. He could go around and do whatever he wanted to, and nobody was there to prevent him from doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were released from Luka camp, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: We were transferred to Batkovic. There was a camp in Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Now we'll turn to the list of some names. May I have Exhibit 12 placed before the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to Exhibit 12, under number 5 is the name of Amir Novalic. Do you know anything about this man? This is Exhibit 13; sorry. Exhibit 13. And the name under number 5.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard a story about Amir Novalic from a young man who was killed during the war. He was at the SUP building when this person was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same document, but Number 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: My apologies to Your Honours and to the Prosecution. My client is asking to be excused to take medicine, and he has stomach pain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll wait for Mr. Jelisic to go out, and then we'll take -- I think he's going to have to leave the courtroom. Mr. Jelisic, can you leave the courtroom, please? And in that time we're going to continue with the examination-in-chief, if the Defence does not object to that. You can leave the courtroom, Mr. Jelisic. Any problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It's for the defendant to decide whether he objects, not us, and we have to take instructions from him whether he agrees or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's correct. Mr. Jelisic, do you authorise your Defence counsel to continue with the examination in chief? This is a --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the defence should go on. I do not object to the continuation of the proceedings at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We thank you. You may leave the courtroom. Please leave the courtroom, Mr. Jelisic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So number 36, Osman Vatic. What do you know about this man?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: This person was also with me at Luka, and then we were transferred to Batkovici, and he was taken from Batkovici to Brcko, I guess home, and we then later heard that he was killed there in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you heard that, but you didn't witness that killing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I only heard about it. I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as Exhibit 12 is concerned, I understand that the witness had opportunity to look at it, and there are no marks that he would recognise any name on that, so I have no questions about this list, Exhibit Number 12. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Greaves? Mr. Didic, you are now going to be asked questions by Defence counsel for Goran Jelisic. Mr. Greaves, are you going to conduct the cross-examination? About how long do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Longer than 15 or 20 minutes, I'm afraid. But what I'm going to try and do is divide it into convenient sections, a small part today and then that which I need on Monday, if that's acceptable to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague wants to speak to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the total amount of time that you think you are going to need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: An hour and a half, because there is extensive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take the liberty of reminding you, Mr. Greaves, that Counts 40 and 41 are absolutely clear. 40 and 41, beatings of Amir Didic. 34: "Between about 20 May and 28 May 1992 at Luka camp, Goran Jelisic beat the Muslim detainee Amir Didic with a police baton, causing Amir Didic to lose consciousness. By these actions, Goran Jelisic committed, Count 40: A violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a)(cruel treatment) of the Geneva Conventions, Count 41: A crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(i)(inhumane acts) of the Tribunal Statute." You have all your rights, Mr. Greaves. I want it to be marked in the transcript, you have all the rights to defend your client, but I would like to recall you to Rule 90(G): "The Trial Chamber shall exercise control over the mode and order of interrogating witnesses," and that you have to bring in the case with genocide. "The cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the direct examination ..." You need an hour and a half in order to reinterrogate a victim who suffered physical beatings that have been recognised and acknowledged by the accused. The witness cannot be able to go home, therefore, will not be able to go home. So we can begin. It's now 15 after 1.00. You have until 1.30, and then you have an hour and a quarter left. But I can tell you, Mr. Greaves, you must remain within the scope of genocide as indicated under Rule 90(H), and if you don't do that, I'm going to have to recall this to you and make you go back to it. The registrar says that Mr. Jelisic does not wish to return but that he come back on Monday at 2.00 in order to hear the rest of your cross-examination, Mr. Greaves. Within the limits we have just set and with full respect for the rights of the accused and the rights of the Defence, please begin your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, I want to ask you about the circumstances of your arrest. You've described that as having taken place on the 19th of May. Can you tell us what it was that you were doing prior to the 19th of May? The reason that I ask you that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this a question which goes to the credibility of the witness, because this was not taken up in the examination in chief. Could you explain how it affects the credibility of the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour has just read out from the agreed statement that it was agreed that this took place on the 12th or 13th of May. There is a dispute as to the date on which this took place, and that is a matter which properly goes to the credibility of the witness, as to whether or not this witness is an accurate, honest, and truthful witness. Therefore, for that reason, I intend to ask him about the date on which he says or claims that these events took place, with Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you can ask the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, just before the Learned Judge interrupted me, I was asking you about events in May 1992. You have claimed that the event took place on the 19th of May, 1992. Can you tell us whether you remember what you were doing in the period between the 1st and the 19th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Between the 1st and 19th of May 1992, I was in home in Palanka, which is where I lived. The bridge was blown up on the 31st of May. I was very tense. It was very tense. The refugees arrived, and there were a lot of refugees in the town where I lived. There were watches there, so people were on guard duties, and this is where I was. People were scared. And I was there until the 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is this, and I want you to deal with it, please. I suggest to you that you were arrested much earlier than the 19th of May, as early as the 11th or 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: No, sir. I was captured on the 19th of May. It was a Tuesday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The persons who arrested you, were those soldiers, or police, or militia, or what?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Approximately, there were six to eight men. There were some in civilians, there were some in camouflage uniforms, and there was one gentleman in a plain police uniform with a short-sleeved shirt. It was about 12.30, 1.00, between Celici and Koraj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you with anybody else? Were other people detained at the same time as you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a friend of mine, Senad Ahmedbasic, called Trnka, and my mother and sister who lives in Koraj. She was at my place, and she wanted me to take her to Koraj because that's where she has a family. Her daughter lived there and she lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The friend of yours that you mentioned, was he a Muslim as well?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were taken from the checkpoint manned by these people to the principal police station in Brcko or to a smaller one?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: They took us to the principal police station in Brcko, there is only one, and they took us to room number 13. It was midway down the hallway to the right. That's the room where they took us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In room 13, you've told us that there were a number of Muslim detainees. Can you help us with this, please? How many people were in the room when you got there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: There were four to five detainees. I recognised one of them. He was Halid, the veterinarian. I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us about his surname? Do you know his surname?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall his name. I know that his first name was Halid. This is how I knew him before the war, and this is still how I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you know where he worked, where his surgery was for being a veterinarian?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know where. They were all working in the field, so he would come to Palanka. I noticed him from before, so I knew him and I knew that he was a veterinarian, but I wouldn't know where his surgery was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was he also taken with you to Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he still alive, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he's alive, and he lives in Upper Rahic. He continues in his job as a veterinarian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were other Muslim detainees brought into the SUP building, the police building, whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were four to six of them -- I cannot tell exactly -- and there were some additional ones which were brought in. So they gathered about 13 to 15 persons, and then we were taken on foot to Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of the ones who were brought in after you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain at the SUP building before being taken to Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Two to three hours, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Luka, you were placed in the first hangar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. First we were searched against the wall of a hangar, and then we were led into the first hangar and we were put into -- taken to the left-hand side there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken into the hangar, was it empty or were there already people there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: The hangar has a sliding door to the right, looking where this metal door is separating it. The left-hand side was empty, and that's where we were put.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it the case that there was nobody in the hangar at all, or there was some but you were put into a different part? I'm sorry, but I don't entirely understand.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: There were people in the other side of the hangar. This side was empty. In the right-hand side, in the corner, there was some things like socks and shirts and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concerning the other people, how many other people were there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Approximately 90 to 100 in the other part of the hangar. When we arrived, they were standing there, and they sang.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of the people who were amongst that group of approximately 90?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: When we were moved to that other part of the hangar, there were some people whom I knew. There was a person from my village who had since moved and lived in Brcko but who was born in my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Osman Hasanbasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the only person that you knew?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: There were others whom I knew from sight, whom I did not know personally but whom I knew from sight. When I saw them, I recognised them. I did not know them personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that group exclusively men or were there women amongst the group?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: They were exclusively men. Only men were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This exclusively male group, would this be right, that it ranged in age from, say, about 18 until 60 or 65; would that be right? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I meant to ask this at the beginning, Mr. Didic, and help me with this if you can, please. During or after the war, did you join the BiH army at any stage?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you volunteer or were you called up into the army?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: When I was released, I went home, and then I joined the BH army in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to know anything at all about where you're living or anything like that, but are you still in the BiH army or have you since left?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: At the end of the war, I left the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, had you taken any part in political life at all? Had you joined any political party?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: No. Before the war, I was not, and I wasn't in any political party during the war, nor since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've anticipated my next questions. I'll return now, if I may, to Luka. What time of day was it that you got there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: You mean at Luka?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Luka, yes. I'm sorry I didn't make that clear, Mr. Didic.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I was brought to Luka from the SUP building around 5.00, 5.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That first evening that you were there, were any people released from the detention facility, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know of that because I didn't see anything. It was growing dark when we were brought in, so I couldn't see what was going on around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any others brought in after your group which had been brought from the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: There were another few people who were brought in also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, were they an exclusively male group?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was one woman among them who was with us in the hangar, but when Osman Vatic was brought in, his wife Sena was also brought alongside, and she was in the office over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I meant to ask you this. The group that had come with you from the SUP building, was that also of a similar make-up to the group that was in the hangar when you got there; in other words, all males between ages of 16 and 60 or so?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, only men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The group that was brought into Luka after you, again was that men, 18 to 60?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, I think we're going to stop at this point --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because you have not yet finished. We will resume on Monday at 2.00. Mr. Didic, you must remain available to the International Tribunal for the weekend, and then we will see one another again on Monday. Thank you for having agreed to do this with as good grace as you did. The Witness and Victims Unit will take care of you during the adjournment. Court stands adjourned, and we will resume on Monday at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 1.32 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 6th day of September, 1999, at 2.00 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
